items.q: **Explain a typical procurement cycle for a company. What are the different activities?**
items.answer:
**Definition first:**
> *"**Procurement is the process of sourcing materials from vendor, inspecting it and finally paying the vendor for the accepted materials.**"*

**The cycle — draw the eight-stage version:**

$$\textbf{Requirement Determination} \rightarrow \textbf{Source of Supply Determination} \rightarrow \textbf{Vendor Selection} \rightarrow \textbf{Order Processing}$$
$$\rightarrow \textbf{Purchase Order Monitoring} \rightarrow \textbf{Goods Receipt} \rightarrow \textbf{Invoice Verification} \rightarrow \textbf{Payment Processing}$$

**The seven-step process list the deck also gives:**
1. **Determining what to buy and how much — Procurement Planning**
2. **Determination of the source of supply**
3. **Selecting the vendor**
4. **Purchase Order (PO) creation**
5. **Goods Receipt (GR)**
6. **Invoice verification**
7. **Processing vendor payment**

---

**Present the activities grouped as four questions** — it shows you understand the structure rather than a list:

| Question | Stages |
|---|---|
| **What do we need?** | Requirement Determination |
| **Who will supply it?** | Source of Supply Determination · Vendor Selection |
| **Order it and chase it** | Order Processing · Purchase Order Monitoring |
| **Did it arrive, and do we owe them?** | Goods Receipt · Invoice Verification · Payment Processing |

**Two closing observations worth marks:**

**① Why it is a cycle, not a line.** Payment does not end the story — **it feeds the next requirement determination**, because the same materials are consumed and bought again.

**② Three of the eight stages are about settling up.** That proportion is not accidental — it is where money moves and where error and fraud live, which is why **three-way matching** concentrates there.

**Note the handoffs at both ends:** the requirement comes from **MRP**, and the payment lands in **Accounts Payable**. **Procurement is the middle of Procure-to-Pay.**

items.q: **How does ERP software help in the different phases of the procurement cycle? How do ERPs help in the purchase order and goods receipt process?**
items.answer:
**The stage-by-stage support table:**

| Cycle stage | **ERP Support** |
|---|---|
| **Procurement Planning** | **auto creation of PR by MRP run** · easy entry of manual PR data · **different planning and lot sizing tools** |
| **Source Determination / Vendor Selection** | **purchase info record** · **scheduling agreement** · **contract** · **auto RFQ creation** · **comparison of vendor quotes** |
| **Purchase Order Creation** | **auto creation of PO from PR, RFQ** · minimum data entry · **automatic price calculation based on conditions** · **electronic PO communication to vendor** |
| **Goods Receipt** | goods receipt in different scenarios · **auto updation of stock and inventory valuation** |
| **Vendor Payment** | **auto matching of invoices with GR qty and PO price** · **blocking of invoices** · **reporting of aging invoices** |

**Group the help into three kinds** — this is what turns the table into an argument:

| Kind | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Don't type it again** | auto PR from MRP, auto PO from PR/RFQ, default values, auto pricing |
| **Don't do the arithmetic yourself** | auto invoice matching, auto stock and valuation update, quote comparison |
| **Don't let a mistake through** | invoice blocking, under/over delivery check, shelf-life check |

> **Re-keying, reconciliation and control** — the entire value proposition of ERP in a transaction-intensive process.

---

**Purchase Order specifically:**
- **Definition:** *"a formal request/document to a vendor to supply certain goods or services under conditions stated in the order"*
- **Converting PR to PO** (or from a previous PO)
- **Reduces data entry and errors**; uses **default values of terms, addresses**
- **Blanket PO** for **consumables**, with **longer period validity**

**Goods Receipt specifically:**
- **Quality inspection and shelf life expiration check**
- **Under / over delivery check and report**
- **Auto updation of stock and inventory valuation**

⚠️ **The GR bullet is doing two different things and both are worth naming.** **Stock update** is a *quantity* movement; **inventory valuation** is a *money* posting that increases stock value on the balance sheet and creates a liability to the vendor. **One physical event, two system consequences, posted simultaneously** — which is the concrete form of *"other areas of ERP transactions have financial implications."*

items.q: **How do ERPs support the vendor payment and invoice verification process? Explain ERS.**
items.answer:
**Invoice verification support:**
- **Invoice entry**
- **Auto or 3-way matching of invoice with GR, and PO**
- **Blocking of invoices** — quality inspection, amount variances, manual blocking/releasing, **parking**
- **Credit / Debit Memos**
- **Invoice Ageing and their reporting**

---

**Three-way matching — explain it properly, it is the core of the answer:**

| Document | Created by | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Purchase Order** | **you** | *what did we agree to buy, at what price?* |
| **Goods Receipt** | **your warehouse** | *what actually arrived?* |
| **Invoice** | **the vendor** | *what are they charging us for?* |

$$\textbf{PO} \wedge \textbf{GR} \wedge \textbf{Invoice} \Rightarrow \textbf{pay}$$

**Match on quantity against the GR; match on price against the PO.** If either fails, the invoice is **blocked**.

**Why three and not two:** any two documents can agree while still being wrong. **PO + invoice agreeing proves the vendor billed what was ordered — not that anything was delivered.** **GR + invoice agreeing proves delivery — not that the price was the one agreed.** Only all three close both gaps.

**Separation of duties is why it works:** the buyer raises the PO, the storekeeper posts the GR, the vendor sends the invoice. **No single person controls all three.**

**Blocking vs parking** — the deck lists both and they differ: **blocked = complete but held** for a variance or pending inspection; **parked = entered but incomplete**, saved without posting. **Credit memos** reduce what you owe (short delivery, returns); **debit memos** increase it.

---

**ERS — Evaluated Receipt Settlement:**

**ERS pays the vendor from the goods receipt and the purchase order alone — without waiting for an invoice.** The system already knows *what arrived* (GR) and *what it costs* (PO conditions), so it computes the amount and pays.

> **ERS is three-way matching with the third document deleted.**

If **PO price × GR quantity** already gives the correct amount, the vendor's invoice adds **no information** — only a document to type in, a document to match, and an opportunity for a mismatch.

**What it requires in exchange:** total agreement on contract prices, and enough trust between the parties that neither needs the invoice as evidence. **That is exactly why ERS sits at level 2 (matured processes) of the procurement maturity model and not level 1** — it is not a feature you switch on, it is a relationship you have to have first.

items.q: **What is a contract? Explain quantity and value contract. What are plant-specific and plant-independent contracts? Explain quota arrangement, delivery schedules and the source list.**
items.answer:
**A contract is a standing agreement with a vendor covering supply over a period**, against which individual orders are released — so terms are negotiated once rather than per order.

**Two axes of classification:**

| Axis | Types |
|---|---|
| **What the contract fixes** | **Quantity contract** · **Value contract** |
| **Who may release against it** | **Central / plant-independent** · **Plant specific** |

**Quantity vs value:**
- A **quantity contract** commits to a **quantity** — *we will buy 10,000 units over the year.* Exhausted when the quantity is delivered.
- A **value contract** commits to a **value** — *we will spend ₹50 lakh with this vendor.* Exhausted when the money is spent.

**Which you use depends on which side is predictable.** For a standard component at a fixed price, **quantity** is natural. For **services** — where *"price comparison is complex"* and one unit of service is not like another — **value is the only unit that means anything.**

**Central vs plant-specific:**
- A **central (plant-independent) contract** can be released against by **any plant** in the company.
- A **plant-specific contract** binds **one plant only**.

> **Central contracts are how a multi-plant company buys as one company** — negotiate once at group volume, let every plant draw on it. This is the procurement answer to Unit 1's Nestlé problem: **29 vanilla records at 29 different prices is what happens when every plant negotiates separately.**

---

**Quota arrangement** — *"required for multiple sources."* It **splits a material's requirement across several approved vendors in fixed proportions** (60% to A, 40% to B), and the system allocates each requisition automatically.

**Why deliberately not buy everything from the cheapest vendor:**
- **Supply risk** — a single source is a single point of failure
- **Negotiating position** — a vendor supplying 100% has all the leverage
- **Capacity** — no single vendor may be able to supply the volume

**The quota is the price of not being hostage to one supplier** — a slightly higher average price bought in exchange for continuity and leverage.

---

**Delivery schedule** — *"for better planning by the supplier."* Three kinds:

| Type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Forecast** | indicative volumes far out — *plan capacity for roughly this* |
| **Detailed** | firmer near-term quantities and dates |
| **Firm** | **committed** |

**Why it is needed:** they are **Unit 3's time fences published outward to the vendor**, so the vendor can distinguish what you are committed to from what you might need. **Without it, the supplier sees only firm orders arriving with your lead time** — and guessing badly means either **excess stock at their end, which you pay for in the price**, or **stock-outs at yours**.

---

**Source list** — **allowed / preferred / blocked suppliers, material-wise.** Its purpose is **control, not convenience**: a vendor whose quality has failed or whose certification has lapsed **must not be orderable**, and relying on every buyer to remember that is not a control. **Note "material wise"** — approval is per material, not per vendor.

items.q: **What are the differences between material and service procurement, and what are the challenges of service procurement? What are the differences of procurement between direct and indirect items?**
items.answer:
**Material vs service procurement:**

| **Material Procurement** | **Service Procurement** |
|---|---|
| **Materials can be inventorized** | **Services can not be inventorized** |
| **Specifications are clearly defined during material procurement** | **Sometimes it is difficult to define a service specification during procurement** |
| **For a given specification price comparison is simple** | **Price comparison is difficult — price may differ by time of purchase, ambience, etc.** |

**Challenges of service procurement:**
1. **Service cannot be inventorized**
2. **Difficult to specify service specifications**
3. **Price comparison is complex**
4. **Goods receipt is replaced by service entry and acceptance**

**All four descend from one fact: a service does not exist as an object.**

| Because a service is not an object… | …this follows |
|---|---|
| nothing to put on a shelf | **cannot be inventorized** |
| nothing to measure or draw | **specification is hard to define** |
| two instances are not identical | **price comparison is complex** |
| nothing arrives at a gate | **GR replaced by service entry and acceptance** |

**The fourth is the most examinable because it is a concrete process change:**

$$\textbf{Service Entry Sheet} \rightarrow \textbf{Acceptance} \rightarrow \textbf{Invoice Verification}$$

**Acceptance is a judgement where goods receipt was a measurement** — which is exactly why service procurement is harder to control. *(The **Service Master / Service Catalog** exists to make specifications reusable, precisely because specifying them freshly each time is the problem.)*

---

**Direct vs indirect items — the full six-row table:**

| | **Direct Items** | **Indirect Items** |
|---|---|---|
| **Demand** | driven by **market demand of end items** | **not driven by end item demand; past consumption trend** |
| **Procurement dept involvement** | **much higher** — must **collaborate with the supplier to design the component** | **much lower** — mostly **off-the-shelf** |
| **Share of spend** | **significant portion by value** | **small portion — typically low value items** |
| **Planning** | **planning runs of MRP or APS** | **consumption based**; sometimes **manual PRs** |
| **Who procures** | **always the procurement team** | **also the end user / employee**, via **E-Procurement or Portal** |
| **Back-end integration** | **much higher** — e.g. delivery schedule releases | **lower** |

**Direct items go into the product; indirect items keep the company running.** That one distinction generates all six rows:

- Because direct items **go into the product**, demand is **derived from what you sell** → MRP planning
- Because they are **part of the product**, their design matters → **collaboration on component design**
- Because a product uses many of them → **large share of spend, high integration**

> **This is Unit 3's dependent vs independent demand exactly.** Direct = **dependent** = **MRP**; indirect = **independent** = **CBP**.

⚠️ **The "who procures" row is the most interesting.** For indirect items, the employee orders their own supplies from a catalogue. **That is a deliberate decision to stop controlling something** — a buyer's time negotiating a ₹500 order costs more than the order. **The right control for low-value items is a pre-approved catalogue with a spending limit, not a purchasing professional.**

items.q: **What are the different types of commodity procurement strategies? Explain auction and hedging. How can procurement strategy differ based on the type of the item?**
items.answer:
**What a commodity is:**
- **Commodities are the items which are not branded and can see wide price variations depending on demand, supply and seasonal variations in price**
- **Commodity procurement is a specialized procurement process**
- **ERPs provide special procurement tools: E-procurement = Auction, and Hedging**

**"Not branded" is the definition and everything follows from it.** If steel from vendor A is interchangeable with steel from vendor B, **there is nothing to compete on except price** — so the buying question inverts from *"which vendor?"* to **"at what price, and when?"**

---

**Auctions:** *"leading ERPs provide **E-procurement / Auction** options that help to get the items at **best price of required quality**."* **Reverse auctions** — where vendors bid the price *down* against each other — appear at level 3 of the maturity model, and only work where the item is genuinely interchangeable, i.e. exactly for commodities.

**Hedging:** *"a common strategy for managing commodity risk. This is done by **taking a position in the futures market that is opposite to the one in the physical market**, with the objective of reducing or limiting risks associated with price changes."*

**How it works:** you are going to **buy** copper in six months, so a **price rise** hurts you. Take the opposite position in futures — a contract that **gains when copper rises**.

$$\textbf{physical loss} + \textbf{futures gain} \approx 0$$

> **You have not made money — you have removed uncertainty.** Hedging converts an unpredictable future cost into a known one, so the company can quote prices to *its* customers without gambling.

**The distinction to state explicitly:**

| | **Auction** | **Hedging** |
|---|---|---|
| Problem solved | *best price **right now**?* | *stop **future** price moves hurting me* |
| Market used | **physical** | **futures** |
| Effect | **discovers** the price | **fixes** the price |

---

**How procurement strategy differs by item type — the four-quadrant matrix**, plotted on **Strategic Impact** × **Financial Impact**:

| Item group | Position | **Driver** |
|---|---|---|
| **MRO** *(indirect goods/services)* | low / low | **"Purchase admin cost should be low"** |
| **Commodities** *(raw material)* | low strategic / **high financial** | **"Price is right"** |
| **Critical Items** *(spares)* | **high strategic** / low financial | **"Should never be out of stock"** |
| **Production Items** *(components)* | high / high | **"Need closer collaboration with vendor"** |

*(**MRO = Maintenance, Repair and Operation supplies**.)*

**The two axes ask genuinely independent questions** — *does this cost a lot?* and *does it stop the business if it goes wrong?* — and the off-diagonal quadrants prove it: **a commodity is a huge budget line but strategically dull; a critical spare may cost ₹2,000 but stops the plant.**

> **The insight the matrix exists to deliver: managing every item the same way is wrong in two different directions.** Negotiating hard on a critical spare is false economy; holding safety stock of commodities ties up cash for nothing.

**Each driver points to a different tool:** admin cost → **blanket POs and employee e-procurement**; price → **auctions and hedging**; availability → **high safety stock, min-max models**; collaboration → **delivery schedules, quota arrangements, eventually VMI**.

items.q: **Explain the procurement maturity model. Explain the different master data for the ERP procurement module and the different KPIs for the procurement process.**
items.answer:
**The procurement maturity model — three levels:**

**Level 1 — Basic Processes:** basic procurement planning · **mostly manual PRs & POs** · purchase order processes · vendor payment · goods receipt · quality inspection

**Level 2 — Matured Processes:** **optimum procurement planning (using MRP or APS)** · **E-procurement** · **ERS for vendor payment** · **basic supplier collaboration** for forecast and inventory

**Level 3 — Innovative Processes:** **sourcing optimization** · **SRM — Supplier Relationship Management** · **auctions and reverse auctions** · **advanced collaboration with suppliers for product development** · **advanced supplier analytics** · **exception management**

**Read the three levels as three relationships with the vendor:**

| Level | The vendor is… | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **1 Basic** | **someone you send orders to** | **transact** |
| **2 Matured** | **someone you share information with** | **collaborate on forecast and inventory** |
| **3 Innovative** | **someone you build products with** | **compete them, analyse them, co-develop** |

> **Transact → share → co-create.**

**Level 1 → 2 is automation** (manual PRs become MRP-driven, paper becomes e-procurement, invoices vanish into ERS). **Level 2 → 3 is strategy** — you stop merely running the process well and start *choosing*.

**That maps onto the chapter's own two definitions of procurement:** level 1 is *"sourcing, inspecting, paying"*; level 3 is *"a strategic approach to optimizing organizational spend."*

⚠️ **Three items are easy to misplace:** **e-procurement is level 2 but auctions are level 3**; **collaboration appears at both** (level 2 *basic*, for forecast and inventory; level 3 *advanced*, for product development); **ERS is level 2**, because it needs price agreement and trust.

**The reliable test: does it need the vendor's cooperation?** If yes, level 2 or above.

---

**Master data for ERP procurement — four objects:**

| Master | Question |
|---|---|
| **Material Master** | **what** are we buying? |
| **Vendor Master** | **who** from? |
| **Terms and Conditions Master** | **on what terms** — payment, delivery? |
| **Service Master / Service Catalog** | **what services**, and how specified? |

**The Service Master exists precisely because of the service-procurement problem** — *"difficult to define a service specification"* — so you specify once and reuse. **The Material Master is shared with production**, seen through the *Purchasing* view rather than the MRP view. **The Vendor Master is the counterpart of the Customer Master** on the sales side.

---

**KPIs for procurement:**

| # | Measure | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Cost Savings** | department's contribution to the financial success of the organization |
| 2 | **Supplier Performance** | performance of suppliers on **price, delivery, quality, service** |
| 3 | **Procurement Cycle Time** | **average time between requisition submission and PO placement** |
| 4 | **Procurement ROI** | **ratio of savings made by operating costs** — measures cost efficiency |
| 5 | **Contract Compliance** | number of exceptions in contract — quantity, price |
| 6 | **Purchasing Analysis** | order value analysis — net order value, **ABC analysis**, frequency analysis |

**In three pairs: money (1, 4) · process (3, 5) · partners and spend (2, 6).**

**Two worth explaining rather than reciting:**

**Procurement ROI** — cost savings alone can always be increased by hiring more negotiators. **ROI asks whether the savings exceeded the cost of finding them.**

**Procurement cycle time is measured requisition → PO, not requisition → delivery.** That boundary is the part procurement actually controls; the vendor's lead time is not theirs to shorten. **A well-chosen KPI stops at the edge of the team's authority.**

items.q: **What are the three levels in the inventory management pyramid? Explain each of them. Explain the four inventory transaction processes.**
items.answer:
**The three levels of the inventory management pyramid:**

| Level | Contents |
|---|---|
| **Strategic Inventory Optimization** *(top)* | **deployment strategy** — strategic locations and how much to hold at each echelon · **channel integration with suppliers** · **adopting best practices like VMI, CPFR, JIT and cross docking** |
| **Inventory Planning** *(middle)* | **using inventory models to determine optimal inventory policies** · **quantitative models for safety stock, cycle stock, cost of inventory** |
| **Inventory Control** *(base)* | **systems to record all inventory transactions** · **cycle counting for inventory accuracy** · **inventory tracking** · **inventory valuation** |

**The deck annotates them Lose · Maintain · Gain, and explaining that annotation is what earns the marks:**

$$\textbf{Transactions \& Control (Lose)} \rightarrow \textbf{Planning (Maintain)} \rightarrow \textbf{Strategic (Gain)}$$

| Level | Label | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Transactions & Control** | **Lose** | doing it well **wins nothing** — it is the price of entry. Doing it badly **loses** money to shrinkage and wrong counts |
| **Inventory Planning** | **Maintain** | correct models and safety stock **keep you competitive** |
| **Strategic Optimization** | **Gain** | VMI, CPFR, cross-docking are where you **beat competitors** |

> **Accurate records are table stakes; strategy is advantage.**

**And the ordering is strictly dependent upward:** you cannot run an inventory model on stock figures that are wrong, and you cannot deploy inventory optimally if you do not know what you have. **That is why it is a pyramid, not three boxes.**

**How ERP supports each level:**
- **Transactions & Control** — goods issue, receipt, stock transfer; **cycle counting for accuracy**; **inventory valuation**; *"help in locating where, how much inventory is lying, of what value"*
- **Planning** — **scientific determination of safety stock, cycle stock**; determining when to order how much; **replenishment planning (ERP tool like DRP)**
- **Strategic** — **Lean, cross docking**; **service-level-based inventory**; **VMI, CPFR**

⚠️ **Note: the deck's slide text elsewhere lists FOUR process groups — Transaction, Control, Planning, Strategic.** That is not a contradiction: **the pyramid merges transactions and control into one base level.** Three pyramid levels, four process groups.

---

**The four inventory transaction processes:**

| Process | Effect on stock |
|---|---|
| **Goods Receipt** | **in** |
| **Goods Issue** | **out** |
| **Stock Transfer** | **sideways** — total unchanged, location changes |
| **Reservations** | **none physically** — the stock is **promised** |

**In · out · sideways · spoken for.** They are exactly the ways stock can change, which is why there are four.

**Goods Receipt:** **ASN from supplier** → receive against PO/delivery schedule → **damage identification** → unload and unpack → **capture lot # details** → **reconcile PO – delivery schedule – GR** → returns if quality unacceptable. **Bar codes and RFID make it simpler and faster.**

> **The ASN comes *before* the goods** — that is its whole point. It lets the warehouse plan labour, dock space and put-away **before the driver is at the gate**. And *"capture lot # details"* is the traceability hook that makes batch management and recalls possible.

**Goods Issue:** **create ASN to customer** → packing and loading → issue and post → **receive POD (proof of delivery)**.

> **Goods issue is goods receipt run backwards** — you *receive* an ASN, they *get* one; you unpack, they pack. **Your goods issue is your customer's goods receipt**, which is the literal meaning of a supply *chain*. **POD matters commercially** — it is the evidence that makes the invoice collectable.

**Reservations** — *"by customer for a later date. Ensure availability."* It moves no goods; it changes **availability, not quantity** — which is what makes an ATP check meaningful.

**Stock Transfer** — **plant to plant, to company, to stores, to warehouse, to dealer.**

⚠️ **"To Company" is not like the others** — it crosses a **legal entity boundary**, so it *is* a sale for accounting and tax even though nothing left the group. That needs **transfer pricing, an invoice, and elimination at consolidation.** **One truck movement; two completely different accounting treatments.**

items.q: **Explain the inventory control processes, including cycle counting, stock valuation and ABC classification.**
items.answer:
**Inventory Control Processes:**
- **Quality Control**
- **Physical Inventory** — *"to match System Inv is a challenge"*
- **Cycle Counting** — **a method of physical inventory counting in periodic intervals**; **policy based on ABC class of items**; **Pareto analysis**
- **Stock Overview** — stocks at different levels, ERP enabled
- **Value Control / Stock Valuation** — **moving average price** · **standard price (in Material Master)**
- **ABC Classification of Materials**

**Why control processes exist at all:** the system's number and the shelf's number drift apart — through **breakage, pilferage, mis-picks, unrecorded issues, deterioration** (all of which reappear as the **shrinkage** KPI). **Control is not about preventing drift; it is about detecting and correcting it often enough that the planning layer above can trust the numbers.**

---

**Cycle counting vs physical inventory:**

| | **Physical inventory** | **Cycle counting** |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | **once a year**, everything at once | **continuously**, a few items at a time |
| Operations | **stop** — the warehouse shuts | **carry on** |
| Error found after | **up to 12 months** | **days or weeks** |
| Effort allocation | **uniform** | **by ABC class** |

**Two independent wins:** errors surface **early**, while the cause is still traceable; and **effort is allocated by value rather than spread evenly.**

$$\textbf{count frequency} \propto \textbf{value at risk}$$

If **A items are 13.3% of items but 60.5% of value**, counting them monthly and C items annually **catches most of the error for a fraction of the effort** — whereas an annual count spends 60% of its labour on the C items carrying 14.5% of the value.

---

**Stock valuation — two methods:**

| | **Moving average price** | **Standard price** |
|---|---|---|
| Stock value | **recalculated on every receipt** | **fixed** at a planned price |
| Price differences | **absorbed into stock value** | **posted to a variance account** |
| Best for | **commodities** | **production components** |

**Standard price is what makes the price-variance posting exist.** The SAP GL document from Unit 3 shows it: **Inventory 245.00 · Goods Received 275.00 · Price Variance 30.00** — received at 275, valued at the standard 245, so **30 goes to variance**.

**Why you want the variance:** product cost stays **comparable month to month**, and purchasing performance shows up **visibly** rather than hidden inside the stock value. *(Standard price lives in the **Material Master** — the Costing/Accounting view.)*

---

**ABC classification** — *"classifying inventory according to annual value of consumption of the items"*, and it **helps in classifying inventory and allocating control efforts as per importance**: **A very important, B moderately important, C least important.**

| Class | **% of value** | **% of items** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **60.5%** | **13.3%** |
| **B** | **25%** | **26.7%** |
| **C** | **14.5%** | **60%** |

**Roughly an order of magnitude difference in value-per-item between an A and a C** — the Pareto principle, measured.

⚠️ **The criterion is annual value of *consumption* — consumption per period × price per unit — not unit price alone.** A **cheap item consumed constantly can be class A**, while an **expensive item bought once a year can be class C**.

**A items justify tight control** — frequent counts, careful reordering, negotiated contracts. **C items justify the opposite** — bulk buying, two-bin systems, minimal attention.

---

**The six classification systems** *(from a slide with no text layer at all — worth reproducing because it is easily missed):*

| Classification | **Full form** | **Criterion employed** |
|---|---|---|
| **ABC Analysis** | **Always Better Control** | **Usage Value** |
| **GOLF Analysis** | **Govt, ordinary, local, foreign** | **Source procurement** |
| **SOS Analysis** | **Seasonal, off seasonal** | **Seasonality** |
| **HML Analysis** | **High Medium Low** | **Unit price — does not take consumption into account** |
| **FSND Analysis** | **Fast, slow, non-monetary, material demands** | **Issues from store** |
| **SDE Analysis** | **Scarce, difficult, easy** | **Procurement difficulties** |

**Six schemes, six different questions about the same item**, each serving a different department: **ABC** for finance and control, **HML** for security and storage, **FSND** for warehouse layout and obsolescence, **SDE** and **GOLF** for procurement, **SOS** for planning.

⚠️ **ABC and HML are the pair most often confused, and the table itself flags the difference** — HML's criterion is *unit price* and it *"does not take consumption into account"*. **A gold-plated bolt bought twice a year is H under HML and C under ABC.**

items.q: **Explain the inventory planning processes and the different inventory models.**
items.answer:
**Two basic drivers for better inventory planning:**

**(i) Never have a stock out** — for **finished goods**: **customer dissatisfaction, lost sales**; for **raw materials**: **production loss**

**(ii) Never carry excess inventory** — **increases cost of operation** · **chance of obsolescence** · **heavy markdown**

$$\textbf{Never stock out} \Rightarrow \text{hold more} \qquad \textbf{Never carry excess} \Rightarrow \text{hold less}$$

> **The two drivers point in opposite directions, and the whole of inventory planning is the compromise between them.**

**"Heavy markdown" is the sharpest cost** — excess inventory does not merely sit there; eventually you **sell it below cost to clear it**, converting a working-capital problem into a realised loss.

**Solutions to overcome / prevent:**
1. **Design better process for replenishment**
2. **Support processing / handling of exceptions**
3. **Scientific approach to reordering — when & how much** — **Q model, P model, Min-Max model, 2-bins model**

---

**Every inventory model answers two questions:**

$$\textbf{WHEN do we order?} \qquad \textbf{HOW MUCH do we order?}$$

| Model | **When** | **How much** |
|---|---|---|
| **Q model (EOQ)** | at the **reorder point** — *variable timing* | **fixed quantity** |
| **P model (periodic review)** | at **fixed intervals** | **variable** — top up to target |
| **Min-max** | at **min** | up to **max** |
| **Two-bin** | when the **first bin empties** | **one bin's worth** |

> **Q fixes the quantity and lets timing float. P fixes the timing and lets quantity float.** The deck states it: P is *"opposite of Q model — qty differs, freq is constant."*

---

**The Q model and EOQ:**

$$\textbf{Total annual cost} = \textbf{annual ordering cost} + \textbf{annual holding cost}$$

**Ordering cost falls as order quantity rises** — each order costs a fixed amount regardless of size, so bigger lots mean fewer orders and the fixed cost spread thinner: $\propto 1/Q$.

**Holding cost rises with order quantity** — bigger orders mean more average stock, and storage, insurance and tied-up capital scale with it: $\propto Q$.

> **One term falls as $Q$ rises, the other rises. Their sum has a minimum — and that minimum is the EOQ.** The deck's curve draws exactly this, with the two lines crossing beneath the total-cost trough.

**Reorder point:**

$$\textbf{Reorder Point} = \textbf{Daily Demand} \times \textbf{Lead Time} = D \times LT$$

**You must reorder while you still have enough stock to survive the lead time.** 50 units/day, 6-day lead time → reorder at **300**.

⚠️ **It assumes demand and lead time are both certain.** Real systems add safety stock: $\textbf{ROP} = (D \times LT) + \textbf{safety stock}$ — and the deck's own P-model diagram shows an **SS** line explicitly.

---

**The P model (periodic review):** at every review, order enough to bring stock back to the target level $M$:

$$Q = M - (\textbf{stock on hand at review})$$

Because stock on hand differs each time, **$Q_1 \neq Q_2 \neq Q_3$** — the *"qty differs"* half of *"opposite of Q model."* The deck's diagram labels **review period $T$, target inventory level $M$, safety stock $SS$**, and three cycles of order → lead time → shipment received.

**When to choose P over Q:** when monitoring is expensive or manual, and especially when **you order many items from one vendor and want one combined delivery** — placing one order instead of forty collapses exactly the fixed ordering and transport cost that EOQ is minimising anyway.

**Its cost:** because you only look on review days, a spike just *after* a review goes unnoticed. **P models need more safety stock — covering the review period *plus* the lead time.**

---

**Min-max** — *pre-define min and max stock level; order when stock on hand is at or near min.* It is a **Q/P hybrid**: order at a reorder point (like Q), order up to a target (like P). **This is what most ERP systems implement as reorder point planning.**

**Two-bin** — *use 2 bins; order when the first bin is empty.* **Min-max with the calculation replaced by a physical fact.** The second bin **is** the safety stock and lead-time cover.

> **Its genius is that it needs no system at all** — no counting, no stock record, no calculation. An empty bin is visible from across the room. **Ideal for class C items, where a planning calculation would cost more than the stock being planned.**

**And it is a pull system** — consumption triggers replenishment, nobody schedules it. **Two-bin is Kanban with bins instead of cards.**

items.q: **What are the strategic inventory management processes? Explain the different KPIs for the inventory process.**
items.answer:
**Strategic Inventory Management Processes — four:**

**1. Process of Inventory Collaboration** — **VMI (vendor managed inventory)**; the **Wal-Mart and P&G** collaboration

**2. Deciding inventory based on service levels** — **critical items, high service levels ⇒ high inventory**; **low service levels ⇒ low inventory**

**3. Best practice processes** — **Cross docking**: *"effective coordination of inbound and outbound shipments"*, example **Wal-Mart**; vendors **SAP, Oracle, Manhattan Associates**

**4. Lean Inventory Management** — **lean principles**, **reduce waste from supply chain**, **Kanban or JIT**

**What makes these "strategic" rather than "planning":**

| Process | What it changes |
|---|---|
| **VMI** | **who decides** the replenishment — the vendor, not you |
| **Service-level-based inventory** | **the target itself** — you choose how often to stock out |
| **Cross docking** | **whether stock is held at all** |
| **Lean / JIT** | **how much waste the chain carries**, end to end |

> **Planning optimises within the rules; strategy changes the rules.** That is why this level is labelled **Gain** while the ones below are **Maintain** and **Lose**.

**Cross-docking, expanded:** in a normal warehouse — *receive → put away → store → pick → ship*. In cross-docking, goods arriving on the inbound dock are **moved straight across to an outbound truck** — no put-away, no storage, no picking. **The warehouse becomes a sorting hub rather than a store**, and what it eliminates is **inventory itself**.

⚠️ **What it costs is slack.** It only works if inbound and outbound schedules are tightly synchronised; **one late truck stalls the flow because there is no buffer stock.** That is why it needs *"channel integration with suppliers"* and cannot be done unilaterally.

**Service levels, expanded:** a service level is the probability of *not* stocking out. **The higher the service level, the more disproportionate the safety stock required** — so the strategic decision is *which items deserve 99% and which are fine at 90%*. **Nobody sets 100%, because 100% requires infinite stock. Accepting some stock-outs is the correct policy**, and choosing where is the strategic act.

---

**KPIs for Inventory Management:**

| Measure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Stock outs** | **# incidents of stock not available when required** |
| **Inventory Turn** | **Annual sales / Average inventory level** |
| **Inventory Carrying Cost** | **Σ all costs of finished goods** |
| **SKU turnover** | **# SKU cycles / turns** |
| **Inventory Ageing** | **Total gross inventory % for specific periods** |
| **Inventory Cycle Counting Accuracy** | **variance between physical and perpetual inventory**, or **# accurate cycle counts / total cycle counts** |
| **Shrinkage** | **costs of breakage, pilferage, deterioration** |
| **Storage space utilization** | **volume of storage / total storage capacity, %** |
| **Obsolescence as % of Total Inventory** | **obsolete & scrap inventory / gross inventory value** |

**Group them by which driver they watch:**

| Driver | KPIs |
|---|---|
| **"Never stock out"** | **Stock outs** |
| **"Never carry excess"** | Inventory Turn · SKU Turnover · Carrying Cost · Ageing · Obsolescence · Storage Utilization |
| **"Are the numbers even true?"** | Cycle Counting Accuracy · Shrinkage |

> **Eight of the nine watch the excess side** — and that imbalance is honest. **Stock-outs are loud** (a customer complains, a line stops) while **excess inventory is silent**, sitting on a shelf until it becomes a markdown. **You need instruments for the failure you cannot hear.**

**Inventory Turn is the headline number.** A turn of 12 means roughly one month of stock on hand; **higher is generally better** because the same sales are supported by less tied-up cash. ⚠️ **But not unboundedly** — push turns up far enough and the **stock-outs** KPI starts rising. **The two are meant to be read against each other.**

⚠️ **Shrinkage and cycle counting accuracy look similar and are not.** Shrinkage measures **the value you actually lost**; cycle counting accuracy measures **how well you know what you have**. **You can have low shrinkage and terrible accuracy** — and that is dangerous in its own right, because the planning layer is running on numbers that are wrong.

items.q: **Explain the typical process steps for an ERP package selection. How is the final package selection done?**
items.answer:
**Why the choice matters:** *"selecting the right ERP package that meets a company's business needs is **one of the most crucial factors for ERP project success**"* — and *"selecting the right ERP solution can be a **make or break** for the success of the ERP project."*

**Packages differ on four axes**, with the deck's own examples:

| Axis | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Strong in a particular process** | **PeopleSoft in HR · BAAN in Manufacturing** |
| **Strong in a particular industry** | **Mincom in Mining · Retek for Retail · Ramco for Utilities** |
| **Database support** | **JD Edwards → DB2 · Oracle → Oracle DB**; **SAP supports all leading databases** |
| **Operating system support** | some run only on **Windows**; others support all leading OS |

---

**The good-fit rule:**
- **No package will meet 100% of the company's needs**
- **Objective is to find a package that is a good-fit (75–80% match) to business requirements and supports long term goals**
- **A good fit gives: lower resistance from users · reduced training needs · less organizational adaptation issues**
- **Gap analysis** figures out the gap between **process, data and user interface requirements** and **ERP offerings**

**Why not 100%:** a package matching everything would have to be **built for you** — and then it is not a package. **The economics of ERP is that development cost is shared across thousands of customers, which only works if the software is standard.**

**Why not 50%:** the missing half must be closed by **customization** (expensive, blocks upgrades) or **changing your processes** (BPR, which people resist).

$$\textbf{fit} \uparrow \Rightarrow \textbf{customization} \downarrow \text{ and } \textbf{organizational change} \downarrow$$

---

**The process steps:**

$$\textbf{Have ERP selection team in place} \rightarrow \textbf{Decide selection criteria and weights} \rightarrow \textbf{Screen initial list and shortlist a few}$$
$$\rightarrow \textbf{Detailed final evaluation of shortlisted vendors} \rightarrow \textbf{Finalize the vendor and enter into contract}$$

**Who does it:** *"a small team comprising **different department heads and company's top management (CIO or CFO)**"*, sometimes with **consultants who know the leading packages well**. The committee **defines the selection process and criteria, attends all vendor presentations, puts relevant questions, does comparative analysis and finally selects.**

**The CIO/CFO presence is the load-bearing part** — delegating a multi-year, organisation-wide commitment to IT alone produces the named failure *"project viewed as an IT project."*

**Tips for dealing with vendors** — each defends against a way of being misled:

| Tip | Defends against |
|---|---|
| ask about **tricky** requirements | a demo tuned to show only strengths |
| run **your** critical business scenarios in their system | a generic demo on clean sample data |
| visit **reference sites** and **hear from the users** | the sales team's account of the last project |
| ask how they **differentiate** | every vendor claiming to do everything |

---

**The two-step process:**

**Step 1 — Screening:** *"evaluation can start with a large number of packages, and based on a set of criteria, **few of them (say two to a maximum of three) are short listed**. This process is called screening."*

**Step 2 — Final selection:** *"these two or three packages are compared against the **list of requirements (100s)** of the company. After the detailed evaluation, one is selected and the company enters into contract."*

**Why two steps and not one:**

$$\textbf{screening: many packages} \times \textbf{few criteria} \longrightarrow \textbf{selection: few packages} \times \textbf{many criteria}$$

> **Cheap criteria eliminate cheaply; expensive criteria are spent only on survivors.** Running hundreds of requirements against twenty packages is thousands of assessments — unaffordable. **The same economics as RCCP vs CRP and ABC-driven cycle counting.**

**And the shortlist size is deliberate:** *two to a maximum of three* — **small enough that detailed comparison is affordable, large enough to retain negotiating leverage right up to contract signature.**

---

**How the final selection is done:**
- **Comparison chart or matrix**
- **Functional requirements match:** **Full or direct match · Partial match · No match**
- **Category of requirements: Vital, Essential and Desirable**
- Scoring based on these parameters plus detailed functional requirements

**It is a two-dimensional grid, and it must be:**

| | **Full match** | **Partial match** | **No match** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Vital** | fine | **serious problem** | **eliminate the package** |
| **Essential** | fine | manageable | costly gap |
| **Desirable** | bonus | fine | fine |

> **A one-dimensional count of matches is misleading.** A package matching 900 of 1,000 looks excellent — until the misses include something **Vital**. Conversely a package missing 200 **Desirable** requirements may be the right choice.

**VED is the requirements-prioritisation counterpart of ABC for inventory and impact levels for risk: rank by consequence, then spend effort accordingly.**

items.q: **What are the criteria for initial package screening? Explain each in a few lines. Why are financial viability and installed base important? What is meant by technology maturity? What types of partnerships can a package vendor have, and why is it an important criterion?**
items.answer:
**Criteria for initial package screening:**

1. **Product Strategy, Vision & Investment in Innovation by Vendor** — is the vendor still developing the product, or milking it?
2. **Financial Viability of the Application Vendor** — will they exist in ten years?
3. **Installed Base and Local Presence** — **geography/country specific · industry domain specific · MNC**
4. **Partnerships** — **implementation partnerships with consulting companies** · **application partnership with third-party applications**
5. **Technology Maturity** — **OS, platform (server, middleware)**
6. **Vendor's Customer Service** — **support strength, upgrades**
7. **Cost of the Software** — **initial capital, AMC, scaling # users** → **TCO = Total Cost of Ownership**

*(The selection diagram adds: **Functionality Fit · Industry Experience · Integration with 3rd party apps · Consulting Partnerships · Local Presence.**)*

**Group them and there are only three questions:**

| Question | Criteria |
|---|---|
| **Does it do the job?** | Functionality Fit · Industry Experience · Technology Maturity · Integration with 3rd party apps |
| **Will the vendor still be here in ten years?** | Financial Viability · Product Strategy & Vision · Installed Base · Partnerships |
| **What will it cost, and who helps us?** | Package Cost / TCO · Customer Service · Local Presence · Consulting Partnerships |

> **Roughly half the criteria concern the vendor as an ongoing institution, not the product** — which follows directly from *"ERP package procurement is not a one-time transaction… **help of the ERP vendor is needed throughout the package life cycle**."* **You are not buying a product; you are entering a decade-long dependency.**

---

**Why financial viability and installed base matter — the deck answers with a list of acquisitions:**

$$\textbf{JD Edwards, PeopleSoft, Siebel, Retek} \longrightarrow \textbf{Oracle} \qquad \textbf{Manugistics} \longrightarrow \textbf{JD Edwards} \qquad \textbf{BAAN, Commerce One} \longrightarrow \textit{gone}$$

| Outcome | Consequence for you |
|---|---|
| **Vendor acquired** | product may be **merged, sunset, or maintenance-only** — features stop, and eventually you are pushed onto the acquirer's platform |
| **Vendor fails** | **no support, upgrades, patches or compliance updates** — on the system running your entire company |

> **The switching cost is what makes this catastrophic rather than annoying.** You cannot change ERP the way you change a text editor — implementation, migration, retraining and process redesign all have to be paid again. **Choosing the vendor is a lock-in decision, so vendor survival is a selection criterion.**

**Installed base is the evidence that answers it:** a large base means the vendor **has revenue**, the product is **proven in real companies**, **skilled consultants are available to hire**, and the vendor **cannot abandon it** without abandoning paying customers.

⚠️ **It must be the *relevant* installed base** — which is why the deck qualifies it three ways. **Ten thousand installations worldwide is no comfort if none are in your country or industry:** local statutory requirements will be unsupported and no local consultant will know the product.

---

**Technology maturity** concerns **OS, platform (server, middleware)** — which operating systems, databases and middleware the package runs on, and how proven that stack is. **A package that runs only on one obscure platform locks you into that platform's fate as well as the vendor's.** Recall that **SAP "supports all leading databases"** while **JD Edwards supports DB2** — that is a maturity difference stated as a fact about breadth.

---

**Partnerships — two kinds, protecting against two different failures:**

**Implementation partnerships with consulting companies** determine **whether you can get the project done at all.** A package with no consulting ecosystem leaves you dependent on the vendor's own limited services arm — expensive, capacity-constrained, and with no competitive pressure on rates. **Many partners means you can run a competitive RFP for the implementation.**

**Application partnerships with third-party applications** determine **what you can connect it to.** No ERP does everything; you will eventually bolt on a specialist CRM, an APS or a tax engine. **Pre-existing certified integrations are the difference between configuration and a custom development project.**

> **Both are network-effect criteria — you are choosing an ecosystem, not a product.**

---

**Cost and TCO:**

| Cost | Nature |
|---|---|
| **Initial capital** — licence, hardware | **one-off**, visible on the quote |
| **AMC** — annual maintenance | **recurring forever**, typically a % of licence value |
| **Scaling # users** | **grows with the company** |

**Two of the three are recurring**, so a package that is cheaper today can be more expensive over ten years.

⚠️ **And the sharpest question on the deck's own evaluation list:** ***"Is the customization cost included in the ERP cost?"*** Almost always **no** — which is precisely how a package that looked cheapest at selection becomes the most expensive by go-live.

items.q: **Give examples and reasons why package selection is sometimes not done in the traditional way. Explain the RFP process of ERP package selection. What are the typical terms of contract with an ERP package vendor?**
items.answer:
**Why companies do not follow the traditional process — four reasons:**

1. **Pressure from major customers to go for a particular ERP so that it can be on the same platform as their customer**
2. **Same ERP for all the companies in the same group, to solve problems of integration / business consolidation**
3. **Price becomes the most dominant factor for ERP selection (especially for SMB)**
4. **Industry specific functionality**

**Three of the four are perfectly rational, and saying so is the mature answer:**

| Reason | Why it is rational |
|---|---|
| **Customer pressure** | if your largest customer requires EDI on their platform, **integration with them may be worth more than a better internal fit** |
| **Group standardisation** | one ERP across a group makes **consolidation, shared services and inter-company transfers** work — a group-level benefit no single-company evaluation would ever measure |
| **Price dominant for SMB** | a small company may simply **not be able to afford** the best-fit package; the real choice is *the affordable one or nothing* |
| **Industry functionality** | if only one package does **oil-field exploration** or **clinical trials**, the evaluation is already over |

> **The common structure: a constraint outside the evaluation outweighs everything inside it.**

**Reason 2 is the direct answer to Unit 1's Nestlé problem** — nine general ledgers and twenty-nine vanilla records arose precisely because divisions chose independently. **Standardising the package is how a group stops that happening again**, and it is worth accepting a worse local fit to get it.

⚠️ **Reason 4 sits awkwardly with the others** — *industry specific functionality* **is** one of the criteria (*Industry Experience*, and the industry-specific installed base). **So it is better described as one criterion dominating all the others** than as skipping the process: when a package is the only one supporting your industry's core process, **the weighted comparison has only one possible outcome.** Hence the deck's own examples — **Mincom in Mining, Retek for Retail, Ramco for Utilities.**

---

**The RFP process for package selection:**

- **Some large organizations follow the RFP (Request For Proposal) process. It is common for large ERP projects**
- **RFP process is a must for Public Sector Organizations**

**A typical RFP document contains:**
- **High Level Scope and Project Duration**
- **Overview of the Company's business and operations**
- **Business benefits the company is expecting from the project**
- **Proposal submission details — when and how the offer is to be submitted**
- **Payment schedule, Bonus, Penalty etc.**

**The five sections exist so that competing bids are comparable:**

| Section | Without it… |
|---|---|
| **Scope and duration** | vendors bid on **different amounts of work**, so prices mean nothing |
| **Business overview** | vendors cannot size the effort — how many plants, users, countries? |
| **Expected benefits** | vendors cannot propose **how** to deliver value, only what to install |
| **Submission details** | bids arrive in different formats at different times — **no fair comparison, no audit trail** |
| **Payment, bonus, penalty** | commercial terms are negotiated separately per vendor, and the cheapest bid may have the worst terms |

> **An RFP is a device for forcing a single question on every bidder so the answers can be laid side by side.** That is why it is a must for public sector organisations: a public body must be able to **prove afterwards** that the process was fair.

**Note that "bonus" appears alongside "penalty."** Penalties for late delivery are expected; **a bonus for early or superior delivery is the less obvious half**, and it exists because a purely punitive contract makes the vendor defensive rather than committed.

---

**Terms of contract with an ERP package vendor — ten salient points:**

1. **Payment terms**
2. **Intellectual property or copyright clauses**
3. **List of deliverables along with software**
4. **How training in the software will be handled**
5. **How the software maintenance will be handled**
6. **How future upgrades will be provided and at what cost**
7. **Software installation help to be provided**
8. **Prerequisites to install** — **hardware specification, operating system, database**
9. **Any audit or review by the package vendor during implementation** — e.g. **final blueprint audit, audit before go live**
10. **License cancellation costs**

**And the framing statement, which is why the list is this long:**
> *"**ERP package procurement is not a one-time transaction with the ERP vendor. Help of the ERP vendor is needed throughout the package life cycle — for supporting the application, for upgrading, for training.**"*

**Sort them by when they bite:**

| When | Clauses |
|---|---|
| **At purchase** | payment terms · deliverables · IP/copyright |
| **During implementation** | installation help · prerequisites · training · **vendor audits** |
| **For years afterwards** | maintenance · **upgrades and their cost** |
| **At the end** | **licence cancellation costs** |

**Only three of the ten concern the purchase itself. Six govern a relationship that outlives the project, and one governs the exit.**

⚠️ **Three clauses hurt most if omitted:**
- **"Upgrades *and at what cost*"** — without a cost commitment you are locked in with no price protection; the vendor knows your switching cost
- **"License cancellation costs"** — negotiate the exit **while you still have leverage**, i.e. before signing. **This is the clause most often left out and most expensive to lack**
- **The vendor's implementation audits** — these are the **vendor checking your implementation**, and you want that agreed in advance rather than discovering it mid-project

items.q: **How is the ERP package market segmented, and who are the players?**
items.answer:
**The market is segmented into three tiers:**

| Tier | Players |
|---|---|
| **Tier 1** | **SAP, Oracle** |
| **Tier 2** | **Microsoft Dynamics, JD Edwards, PeopleSoft, Infor, IFS, Epicor, Lawson** *(also **QAD**)* |
| **Tier 3** | **small players, local players** — *"several small ERPs"* |

**The vendor landscape with products:**

| Vendor | Products |
|---|---|
| **SAP** | **All-in-One** *(medium size companies)* · **Business One** *(small companies)* |
| **Oracle** | **PeopleSoft · JD Edwards · Siebel** |
| **Others** | **Infor · IFS · Epicor · Microsoft · Ramco** |

**For SMBs: preconfigured templates — reduces time and cost of implementation.**

---

**Two observations that lift this beyond a list.**

**① The two big vendors' product lists tell two different growth stories.** **SAP's names are tiers of its own product** — All-in-One and Business One are SAP-built offerings aimed downward. **Oracle's names are companies it bought** — PeopleSoft, JD Edwards and Siebel were all independent vendors. **SAP grew organically; Oracle grew by acquisition.**

That is exactly the list the **financial viability** criterion used as its warning — **every one of Oracle's product names here is a former competitor that stopped being independent.** **PeopleSoft is the sharpest case**, since the same deck opened by naming it *"very strong in Human Resource"*: **being the best in a niche did not keep it independent.**

**② The tiers segment by customer size, not by quality** — and treating them as a quality ranking is the standard mistake:

| Tier | Typical customer | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **large enterprises, MNCs, multi-country** | broadest functionality, highest cost, longest implementations |
| **2** | **mid-market, large single-country** | narrower scope, faster and cheaper |
| **3** | **small and local** | often country- or industry-specific, minimal cost |

**A Tier 1 package is frequently the *wrong* choice for a small company** — *price becomes the most dominant factor for SMB*, and **TCO** grows with the tier. **And the reverse holds:** Tier 3 will not support multi-country statutory reporting or multi-currency consolidation.

> **The tier that fits is the one whose customers look like you** — which is exactly why the screening criteria demand an installed base that is **geography specific, industry domain specific, and MNC** where relevant.

**Evidence for the tier structure, from the deck's image-only comparison table:** industry-specific software — **SAP 25 industries · Oracle 23 industries · Microsoft Dynamics AX 4 industries.** **Breadth of industry coverage is what Tier 1 is actually selling.**

⚠️ **Note that JD Edwards and PeopleSoft appear in Tier 2 while also being Oracle products.** Both are true: **they still compete in the mid-market, but the company behind them is now a Tier 1 vendor.** **Acquisition moves a product between tiers without removing it** — and for the customer, the roadmap, support model and upgrade path all changed even though the software did not.

items.q: **What things need to be considered for an ERP partner selection? Define an approach to develop a selection matrix. What can be the components of an RFP for selecting a consulting partner?**
items.answer:
**Why it matters, and why there may be several partners:**
- **Selecting the right consulting partner is crucial for ERP project success**
- **There can be different consulting partners for different phases** — *one for package selection · a second for package implementation · a third for all technical works from a low cost country*
- **Large global implementations these days are mostly broken between multiple partners**
- **When multiple partners are involved, coordination between different players becomes extremely important**

**Why hire three firms instead of one:**

| Partner | Why a *different* firm |
|---|---|
| **Package selection** | a firm that also sells implementation has **an interest in which package you pick**. **Separating selection from implementation removes the conflict** |
| **Implementation** | the bulk of the work; needs deep **product** expertise |
| **Offshore technical work** | development and testing are **cost-sensitive and location-independent** |

**And the deck immediately names the price:** *"coordination between different players becomes extremely important."* **Every boundary between firms is a boundary where work can fall through and nobody owns the outcome end to end** — which is exactly why **"Ability to Provide End-to-End Service"** is one of the ten criteria.

**The selection effort:** team of **4–10 people, could be 60 for large organizations**; time **two to six months, up to one year is not unusual**; use **reports from consultancy firms**; **follow a selection process**.

---

**The ten selection criteria:**

1. **Vendor's Industry Experience**
2. **Process Consulting Experience**
3. **Client Reference and Client Satisfaction Level**
4. **Ability to Provide End-to-End Service**
5. **Quality of Project Management**
6. **Quality of Tools and Methodologies**
7. **Presence in Different Geographies**
8. **Global Delivery Capability**
9. **Reputation and Branding**
10. **Price and Value for Money**

**Group them:**

| Group | Criteria |
|---|---|
| **What do they know?** | Industry Experience · Process Consulting Experience |
| **How do they work?** | Quality of Project Management · Quality of Tools and Methodologies · End-to-End Service |
| **Can they reach us?** | Presence in Different Geographies · Global Delivery Capability |
| **What do others say, and what does it cost?** | Client Reference & Satisfaction · Reputation and Branding · Price and Value for Money |

> **Know · work · reach · reputation.**

**Compare against the package criteria — the difference is examinable:** package criteria are dominated by *"will the vendor survive?"* (financial viability, product strategy, installed base); **partner criteria are dominated by *"can these people actually deliver?"*** (experience, methodology, project management). **You buy a package for a decade and assess the vendor as an institution; you buy a partner for a project and assess capability to execute.**

⚠️ **"Presence in Different Geographies" ≠ "Global Delivery Capability."** *Presence* means offices and people **where your sites are**; *global delivery* means they can **run work across locations**, moving it offshore and coordinating time zones. **Being in many places is not the same as being able to work across them.**

⚠️ **"Price and Value for Money" is deliberately not just "Price"** — the cheapest bid on a project where *"poor project team skills"* and *"ineffective vendor and consultant"* are named failure causes is a false economy.

---

**An approach to develop the selection matrix:**

1. **Assemble the selection team** (4–10 people; up to 60 for very large organisations)
2. **Agree the criteria** — the ten above, plus any specific to your industry or geography
3. **Assign weights** to each criterion reflecting its importance to this company — an MNC weights *global delivery* heavily; a single-country firm does not
4. **Define a scoring scale** and the evidence that will justify a score — **client references, site visits, methodology documents, rate cards**
5. **Score each shortlisted partner** against every criterion
6. **Compute weighted totals**, but **review the raw scores too** — a partner scoring zero on a critical criterion should not be rescued by a high total
7. **Use the matrix to shortlist, then negotiate** — selection is not finalisation

**This is the same weighted-score structure as package selection**, and the same caution applies: **a single weighted total can hide a fatal gap**, which is why package selection added the **Vital / Essential / Desirable** dimension.

---

**Components of an RFP for selecting a consulting partner:**

- **High level scope and project duration**
- **Overview of the company's business and operations**
- **Business benefits the company is expecting from the project**
- **Proposal submission details — when and how the offer is to be submitted**
- **Payment schedule, Bonus, Penalty**

**Sections of a typical RFP:** **scope of project · duration of project · payment terms with schedule · performance bonus/penalty clause**

**Bids are evaluated on two dimensions: Technical and Financial.**

**The process steps:** **RFI outputs (optional) → RFP Preparation → RFP Release** *(to selected vendors, with **conference call, common meeting, media advertisement**)* **→ Response Collection → Evaluation → Partner Selection → Contract Negotiations → Partner Finalization → Contract Signing → Project Kick off**

**Three details worth noting:**

**① The RFI is optional and comes first** — a cheap request for basic information used to cut a long list to a shortlist before anyone writes a full proposal. **RFI shortlists; RFP selects.**

**② Release is not just sending the document.** Conference call and common meeting exist so **every bidder hears the same clarifications at the same time**; **media advertisement** makes the process **open** rather than invitation-only, which is why it is mandatory in the public sector.

**③ Selection and finalization are separate, with negotiation between them** — **you are selected-but-not-final while terms are negotiated**, which is deliberate leverage: if negotiations fail, you can still turn to the runner-up.

items.q: **What are the advantages and disadvantages of having an in-house ERP consulting team vs an outside partner? What type of activities can be done from offshore, and in what phase how much? How is the ERP consulting market segmented?**
items.answer:
**In-house Implementation — Advantages:**
- **Need not pay external consultants**
- **Team may have better process knowledge**

*(The pros diagram adds: **better industry knowledge**, **no money goes outside**.)*

**In-house Implementation — Disadvantages:**
- **External consulting team will have better package knowledge** *("Product Expertise")*
- **In-house team do not have access to methods and tools which a consulting company brings as part of their implementation methodology**
- **Implementation is not their core competency**
- **May lack on ERP project management skills**
- **Overall may not work out to be cost effective if all internal costs are factored**
- *(diagram adds)* **No implementation experience** · **High chances of failure**

**Where it may work:**
- **Better suited for roll outs**
- **Some help from external consultants on specific areas**
> *"In-house implementation may work in case of **Rollout projects** where implementation in the first site had been done by the consulting team and subsequent rollout by the in-house team."*

---

**The trade is one kind of knowledge against another:**

| | **In-house team has** | **External team has** |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge of… | **the business** — its processes, exceptions, politics | **the package** — how to configure it |
| Plus | industry knowledge | **methods and tools**, implementation experience, **project management skill** |

**Neither side has both — which is why the standard project team has two halves**, as the project-team chapter says: *"the two teams complement each other skill-wise."* **So "in-house vs external" is a slightly false framing;** the real question is **how much external help you need on top of the core team you will have regardless.**

**The strongest disadvantage is the one that sounds weakest:** *"implementation is not their core competency."* **An internal IT team implements an ERP once; a consulting firm has done it fifty times** — which is why they have accumulated **methods and tools**, the compressed experience of prior projects, which you cannot buy separately.

⚠️ **Note the deck contradicts the in-house team's own headline advantage.** *"No money goes outside"* is listed as a pro, but *"may not work out to be cost effective **if all internal costs are factored**"* is a con. **That is the point: the saving is visible (no invoice) while the cost is invisible** — senior staff off their day jobs for a year, a longer timeline, rework from inexperience. **The apparent saving is an accounting artefact of which costs get billed.**

**Which is why rollouts are the one place it genuinely works:** the consultants already built and proved the template at site one, so **site two is repetition, not design. The hard part — the blueprint — has already been paid for.**

---

**Offshoring — phase-wise:**

| Project Phase | **% on-site** | **% offshore** | **Type of activity from offshore** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Project Preparation** | **100%** | **0%** | — |
| **Business Blueprint** | **90%** | **10%** | **PoC / demo scenarios, blueprint documentation (partial)** |
| **Realization** | **30%** | **70%** | **Configuration, Testing, Development** |
| **Final Preparation and Go Live** | **50%** | **50%** | **Data migration, End user training, Content preparation** |
| **Support** | **20%** | **80%** | **Resolving issues, routine utility jobs, system development, change requests** |

**Commonly offshored:** **development · unit testing, volume testing · training content preparation · support**
**Offshorable to a limited extent:** **configuration · data migration**
**Difficult to offshore (done on-site):** **business blueprinting · integration testing · UAT · end user training · change management activities**

**The curve 0% → 10% → 70% → 50% → 80% has a clear shape:**

$$\textbf{offshore \%} \propto \frac{1}{\textbf{customer contact required}}$$

| Phase | Why |
|---|---|
| **Preparation 0%** | kickoff, charter, team formation — pure relationship-building |
| **Blueprint 10%** | **workshops with business users**. **You cannot elicit requirements from another continent** |
| **Realization 70%** | configuration, development, testing **against a signed blueprint** — the requirement is written down, so location stops mattering |
| **Go Live 50%** | splits — data and content travel; **training and cutover do not** |
| **Support 80%** | ticket-driven and repeatable; **time-zone difference becomes an advantage** |

> **Work that is *specified* can be offshored; work that is *discovered* cannot.**

**The dip at Go Live is the informative point** — offshore share falls from 70% back to 50% precisely because go-live is when **people, not systems, need attention.**

⚠️ **Unit testing is offshorable; integration testing and UAT are not** — and the reason is precise. **Unit testing** checks *does this configuration do what the spec says?* — self-contained. **Integration testing** needs cross-module business judgement. **UAT is by definition the business users deciding whether they accept it — it cannot be offshored because the people doing it are the customer.**

**Two abbreviations:** **ODC = Offshore Development Center · GDC = Global Delivery Center**

---

**The ERP consulting market — three tiers:**

| Tier | Companies |
|---|---|
| **Tier 1** | **IBM, Accenture, SAP** |
| **Tier 2** | **Capgemini, Deloitte, HP, CSC, TCS, Infosys, Wipro** |
| **Tier 3** | **HCL-Axon, Siemens, Cognizant, L&T Infotech, Atos, smaller companies, local players like Ramco** |

**Two observations:**

**① SAP appears in Tier 1 of the consulting market as well as the package market** — the vendor sells implementation services for its own product, which is exactly why some companies deliberately hire **a different firm for package selection** than for implementation.

**② The Indian IT services firms are spread across Tiers 2 and 3** — **TCS, Infosys, Wipro** at Tier 2; **HCL-Axon, Cognizant, L&T Infotech** at Tier 3. That distribution is **the offshoring table made into an industry**: the phase-wise percentages (70% of Realization, 80% of Support) describe exactly the work these firms built their ERP practices on, and **ODC/GDC is the operating model that delivers it.**

**As with packages, the consulting tiers mean customer size, not quality.** A Tier 1 firm brings global delivery capability and multi-geography presence at a price only a large programme can justify.

items.q: **Explain the nine levers of project scope. What is meant by process scope and application scope? What is interface scope — give common examples. What are master and transaction data objects for data migration? Give examples of technology scope and scope exclusion.**
items.answer:
**The nine levers of ERP project scope:**

| Lever | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Location Scope** | which **sites, plants, countries**? |
| **Business Scope** | which **legal entities / business units**? |
| **Process Scope** | which **business processes** — P2P, O2C, H2R? |
| **Application Scope** | which **modules** — FI, MM, SD, PP, HR? |
| **Interface Scope** | which **other systems** must we connect to? |
| **Report Scope** | which **reports** will we build? |
| **Data Migration Scope** | which **data objects**, and how much history? |
| **User Scope** | **how many users**, of which roles? |
| **Technology Scope** | which **platform, OS, database, landscape**? |

> **Identify in-scope and out-of-scope items clearly (and get sign off)!**

**A lever is something you can pull to make the project bigger or smaller**, and every one is independently adjustable. **That is the practical value: when a project is over budget, you do not have nine hundred choices, you have nine** — drop two locations, defer a module, cut the report list, migrate two years of history instead of seven.

**The instruction matters more than the list.** Writing down what is **out** of scope is harder and more valuable than what is in — because *"frequent change in scope"* is a named ERP project risk and **scope creep** is a named technology-project risk. **An unstated exclusion is an assumed inclusion.**

**Examples of scope exclusion:** modules deliberately deferred to a later phase; plants not in this rollout; legacy reports that will not be rebuilt; interfaces to systems being retired; historical data older than the agreed cutoff; user groups who will keep using the legacy system.

**Examples of technology scope:** the **operating system and database**, the **server and middleware platform**, the **system landscape** (development, quality, production), **authorization standards**, and the hardware prerequisites the vendor contract specifies.

---

**Process scope vs application scope — the pair most often confused:**

- **Process scope is horizontal** — it follows a **business process end to end**, across whatever modules it touches. *Procure-to-Pay* runs through **MM** (requisition, PO, goods receipt) and **FI** (invoice, payment).
- **Application scope is vertical** — it names **which modules are implemented**. *FI, CO, MM, SD.*

⚠️ **You can implement a module without implementing every process that uses it, and you can implement a process spanning modules you are only partly deploying.** That mismatch is where scope gaps hide: a project scoped as *"MM and FI"* may quietly omit the **service procurement** process even though both its modules are in.

> **Scope by process, verify by application** — or you will find the gap at integration testing.

---

**Interface scope — common ERP interfaces:**
- **Interface with Design Systems**
- **Interface with Shop Floor Control Systems**
- **Interface with Point Of Sale Systems**
- **Interface with Weigh Bridge Application**
- **Interface with Laboratory Management Information Systems**
- **Interface with Industry Application**

**Every one is a system that exists because the ERP cannot do that job:**

| Interface | Why a separate system exists |
|---|---|
| **Design systems (CAD/PLM)** | engineering design is a different discipline — and the **EBOM** originates there |
| **Shop floor control** | **real-time machine control**; ERP works in transactions, not milliseconds |
| **Point of Sale** | **retail till hardware** that must keep working when the network is down |
| **Weigh bridge** | a **physical instrument** producing a measurement |
| **LIMS** | **laboratory instruments and test protocols** |

**Three of the six are essentially instruments — weigh bridge, shop floor, LIMS — reading physical reality into the ERP.** The weigh bridge is the cleanest example: **a truck's weight determines the goods receipt quantity**, so the scale must post directly into the GR or someone will type it in wrongly.

**Interface scope is a lever because each interface is a small development project** with its own specification, testing and failure modes.

---

**Data migration objects:**

**Master Data Migration Objects:** **Material Master · Customer Master · Vendor Master · Asset Master · Chart of Accounts · Cost Centres / Profit Centres / Cost Elements · Pricing Condition Master · Bill of Material, Routing, Work Centres · Plant Maintenance Masters · Quality Management Masters · Warehouse Master**

**Transaction Data Migration Objects:** **GL Balances & Open Items · Customer Open Items · Vendor Open Items · Budget Values · Loans and Advances · Open Internal Orders · Stock Balances · Material in Transit (High Seas, On Port) · Open Service Contracts & Orders · Open Contracts & Purchase Orders · Open Sales Contracts & Orders**

**The distinction:**
- **Master data describes things that persist** — a material, a customer, a cost centre. **Created once, referenced many times.**
- **Transaction data records events** — an order, a receipt, a payment. **Created constantly, references master data.**

> **The word "open" appears seven times in the transaction list, and it is the whole principle: you do not migrate history — you migrate what is unfinished.**

$$\textbf{migrate} = \textbf{the state the business is in}, \text{ not } \textbf{the story of how it got there}$$

A purchase order already delivered and paid affects nothing going forward; **an open PO must move**, because goods will still arrive against it.

**"Material in Transit — High Seas, On Port" is the vivid case:** goods that have left the vendor and not yet arrived, sitting on a ship. **Owned, payable, on nobody's shelf** — and if you miss them at cutover, both stock and payables are wrong on day one.

**The master/transaction split matters practically** because they migrate at different times: **master data can be loaded weeks ahead and validated; open transaction data can only be extracted at the very last moment**, once the legacy system stops. **That is the whole reason cutover is a distinct, minutely-planned phase.**

items.q: **Explain the different components of an ERP project plan. What are the components of a project-resource plan? What are the standards and processes for an ERP project? Explain the parts of a project charter.**
items.answer:
**The project plan:**
