- **Project plan depends on the implementation strategy of the company**
- **Granularity depends at which point it is created and for which audience**
- **Typically prepared in a spreadsheet (like Excel) or with tools like MS Project**

**An ERP project plan is composed of several plans:**
1. **Activity, Deliverables and Milestone plan**
2. **Resource plan**
3. **Training Plan**
4. **Testing Plan**
5. **Data Migration Plan**
6. **Change Management Plan**

**Five of the six are named after the things that most often go wrong** — and pointing that out is the strongest framing:

| Sub-plan | Guards against |
|---|---|
| Activity / Deliverables / Milestones | *"lack of planning of scheduling, resources and activities"* (**39%**) · *"milestones not being set"* (**29%**) |
| Resource plan | *"inadequate co-ordination of resources"* (**26%**) |
| Training plan | *"inadequate training"* · *"training issues for the team"* |
| Testing plan | *"no quality control"* (**34%**) |
| Data migration plan | *"having clean data in the system"* |
| Change management plan | *"inadequate change management"* · *"employees resist ERP implementation"* |

---

**Project Resource Plan — components:**
- **In which month how many resources are needed**
- **Whether resources need to be at client site or at an offshore location**
- **How many resources from the consulting company side and how many from the core team**
- **Ramp up / Ramp down plan**
- **Resource Plan is derived from Project Plan**
- **Different roles are introduced during different phases**

**Four dimensions, each mapping to something already established:**

| Dimension | Connects to |
|---|---|
| **When** — which month | the **phase plan** |
| **Where** — site or offshore | the **offshoring percentages** — 0/10/70/50/80 by phase |
| **Whose** — consulting or core team | **in-house vs external** — product knowledge vs business knowledge |
| **Ramp up / down** | different roles in different phases |

> **"Resource Plan is derived from Project Plan" is the causal direction, and getting it backwards is the classic error.** You plan the work and then compute the people it needs. **Staffing to availability rather than to plan is how *aggressive time frame* becomes an unachievable schedule.**

**Ramp-up/ramp-down is why the plan is monthly:** Preparation needs a handful of people; **Realization needs the peak** (configuration, development and testing at once); Go Live needs trainers and data people; Support needs a small steady team. **A flat headcount would be idle at both ends and short in the middle.**

**Implementation time depends on:** **number of sites · number of modules or functions · maturity level of the organization · customization.** **Three of those four are scope levers by another name** — the duration is a function of the scope. *("Maturity level" is the one that is not a lever, and you cannot shorten the project by wishing it away.)*

---

**Project Standards and Procedures — nine:**
1. **Change request management standards**
2. **Issue management standards**
3. **Project communication management standards**
4. **Project monitoring and status reporting standards**
5. **Testing standards**
6. **System configuration standards**
7. **Development strategy and standards**
8. **Authorization standards**
9. **Project documentation standards** — formats for **WSRs, Module Status Reports, MoMs, Issue Log, Charter, Functional Specs, Tech Specs, Test plans/scripts, Risk Register, Naming and Versioning Standards**

*(**WSR** = Weekly Status Report · **MoM** = Minutes of Meeting)*

**Standards exist because an ERP project is done by dozens of people across several firms and locations** — without agreed formats, **nothing can be compared, aggregated or handed over.** Three concrete consequences:

- **Naming and versioning standards** — without them, two consultants create the same object twice under different names, and nobody knows which functional spec is current
- **Status reporting standards** — if every module lead reports differently, **the PM cannot roll them up into one view**, and *"mismanagement of progress"* follows mechanically
- **Configuration and development standards** — the system will be **maintained for a decade by people not on this project**

> **Standards are the cheapest possible control** — they cost a document each and prevent a whole class of problems, which is why they belong in Project Preparation, before there is anything to standardise.

---

**The Project Charter — a major deliverable of the Project Preparation phase**, containing:
- **Project overview** — **SoW, Objectives, Benefits; Vision and Mission statements**
- **Project scope**
- **Project goals and objectives**
- **Project deliverables**
- **Business case summary**
- **Total estimated project cost**
- **Implementation strategy**
- **Project stakeholders**
- **Assumptions and constraints**
- **Risk assessment**

**It is presented formally at the Kick Off Meeting.**

**The charter is the project's constitution — one document fixing what we are doing, why, who decides, and how we will work:**

| Charter section | Fixes |
|---|---|
| overview, business case, benefits | **why** |
| scope, deliverables, goals | **what** |
| stakeholders, organisation and roles | **who decides** |
| implementation strategy, plan, standards | **how** |
| assumptions, constraints, risk assessment | **what could go wrong** |

> **"Assumptions and Constraints" carries the most weight in practice.** Every estimate rests on assumptions — *the legacy data is clean*, *the core team is full-time*, *there will be one site go-live*. **Writing them down converts an argument later ("you should have known") into a fact ("this assumption failed, here is the impact").**

**A real charter's table of contents** runs: **1 Introduction** *(SoW, objectives, benefits, assumptions and constraints)* · **2 Scope** *(functional, technical: software and hardware)* · **3 Project Organisation and Roles** *(executive sponsor, executive committee, steering committee, project manager, integration manager, project office, team leads)* · **4 Project Plan** *(methodology, scope/issue/complexity/risk management, planning and monitoring, QA; implementation, training, knowledge transfer, change management)* · **5 Standards and Procedures** *(monitoring, configuration, communication plan, system landscape, authorisation standards, error handling, enhancement approval)*.

**Note that the charter contains the standards, plans and risk assessment by reference** — it is the **single approved artefact from which everything else hangs**, which is exactly why presenting it *is* the kick-off.

items.q: **What are the typical risks of an ERP project? Explain the five steps of the risk management process.**
items.answer:
**Definition:** **a risk is the threat or probability that an action or event will adversely affect the project.**

**Impact levels:**

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Negligible** | **leading to minor inconvenience** |
| **Marginal** | **leading to degradation of secondary mission** |
| **Critical** | **leading to serious threat to primary objective** |
| **Catastrophic** | **leading to failure of primary mission** |

> **Identify all critical and catastrophic threats to the project and deal with them proactively.**

**The instruction is where the value is:** you are explicitly told **not** to actively mitigate negligible and marginal risks — they are logged and watched. **That is the same attention-allocation principle as ABC for inventory, VED for requirements and cycle counting by class: rank by consequence, then spend effort where the consequence justifies it.**

---

**Reasons for ERP Project Risk:**

**Frequent change in scope · Aggressive Time Frame · Connectivity in remote location · Computer Literacy of Employees · Organizational Politics · Lack of Top Mgmt Support · New Technology · No Prototyping · Inexperienced Core Team**

**Group them and three sources appear:**

| Source | Risks |
|---|---|
| **The project was set up badly** | frequent change in scope · aggressive time frame · **no prototyping** |
| **The organisation is not ready** | computer literacy · organizational politics · lack of top mgmt support · inexperienced core team |
| **The environment is hostile** | connectivity in remote locations · new technology |

**Four of the nine are about people and the organisation, not software** — which is the recurring lesson of this course.

**"No prototyping" is the least obvious:** without a prototype, **users first see the system at UAT**, when configuration is done and changing it is expensive. **A prototype converts a late, expensive surprise into an early, cheap one.**

**"Aggressive time frame" is the risk that manufactures other risks** — compress the schedule and testing, training and data cleansing all get cut.

---

**The three-tier risk taxonomy** *(this entire taxonomy exists **only as an image**; the slide carries no text at all):*

**Risk associated with EVERY project:** **low user involvement · poor project team skills · low top management support · poor project monitoring · ineffective project management techniques · scarcity of resources · changing external environment · attrition**

**Risk associated with a TECHNOLOGY project:** **inadequate management of IT issues · scope creep · volatile IT system · instable vendor**

**Risk associated with an ERP project:** **implementation strategy · inadequate selection · ineffective communication system · inadequate change management · ineffective vendor and consultant · inadequate training · inadequate business process reengineering · inappropriate implementation strategy · complexity of the ERP system · inadequate legacy system management**

**The three tiers are cumulative:**

$$\textbf{every project} \subset \textbf{technology project} \subset \textbf{ERP project}$$

> **An ERP project carries all twenty-two risks, not just the ten in its own tier** — and that explains why ERP projects fail more often than ordinary projects.

**And the ERP-specific tier is almost entirely about the organisation, not the software:**

| ERP-specific risk | Points back to |
|---|---|
| **inadequate selection** | the package and partner selection chapters |
| **inadequate BPR** · **inadequate change management** | Unit 2 in its entirety |
| **inadequate training** · **ineffective communication** | the change management plan |
| **ineffective vendor and consultant** | partner selection criteria |
| **inadequate legacy system management** | data migration and interface scope |
| **complexity of the ERP system** | the good-fit rule and customization |

**Nine of the ten are things this course has already taught you to prevent.** Only *"complexity of the ERP system"* is inherent to the product.

---

**The Five Step Project Risk Management Approach:**

1. **Find potential risk elements of the project**
2. **Assess the probability of occurrence of these risk elements**
3. **Analyze impact of each of these elements**
4. **Prioritize the risk**
5. **Develop a risk mitigation plan for top risk elements**

**Steps 2 and 3 are separate on purpose, and step 4 is what joins them:**

$$\textbf{risk exposure} \approx \textbf{probability} \times \textbf{impact}$$

**Neither factor alone tells you what to do.** A catastrophic risk that is nearly impossible and a marginal risk that is certain can carry the same exposure, and both are handled differently from a critical risk that is likely.

**Step 5 says "for TOP risk elements", not all** — mitigation costs money and attention, and you buy it only for the risks that justify it. **The other risks stay on the Risk Register, watched.** *(The Risk Register appears in the documentation-standards list — the artefact where steps 1–4 live, maintained through the project rather than produced once.)*

---

**The Risk Management Plan:**
- **Contain the risk exposure once the risk has occurred**
- **Explore business processes that may be changed to adapt to the ERP system**
- **Explore ERP modules that may need changes**
- **Assess the feasibility of the changes**
- **Estimate the cost, time, and the resources required**
- **A phased approach to ERP implementation to contain the exposure**

**The first bullet is about *containment*, not prevention** — a mature position: some risks will materialise regardless, and the plan's job is to limit the damage.

**Bullets 2 and 3 are the two ways to close any gap:**

$$\textbf{change the business process} \qquad\text{or}\qquad \textbf{change the ERP module}$$

**Adapt to the software, or adapt the software.** The first is BPR; the second is customization. **Bullets 4 and 5 price both** — *feasibility*, then *cost, time and resources* — so the choice is made on evidence. **And the course's standing advice is clear on which usually wins:** *"minimize developments and customization… use the standard software."*

**The phased approach is the strongest structural mitigation.** Going live in one plant, or with one module, **contains a failure to that scope** — you learn, correct, and roll the corrected version onward. **Big bang converts every risk into a single, simultaneous, all-or-nothing event.**

**Mitigate the Risk — the four named remedies:** **appropriate selection team · right selection process · adequate budget · adequate time allocated.** **Three of the four are simply "do not rush the selection"** — earned emphasis, given that *"inadequate selection"* and *"poor ERP package selection"* appear on both the risk taxonomy and the failure list.

items.q: **What are critical success factors for an ERP project? Why do ERP implementations succeed or fail? Illustrate with real case studies.**
items.answer:
**What a CSF is:**
- **These are the factors vital for the success of an ERP project. If addressed, CSFs improve the chances for success significantly**
- **CSFs have been divided into strategic and tactical factors**, further divided into **strategic, tactical, operational, organizational and technological**
- **CSFs can also be looked at from the perspective of stakeholders**

**Categories of CSFs:** **careful selection of ERP package and implementation partner · clear goals and objectives · project management · interdepartmental communication and co-operation · training and change management · project team competence · top management support · vendor support · organizational characteristics · ERP system · user involvement · project monitoring · environment · implementation strategy · software development**

**A CSF is not a task — it is a condition.** *"If addressed, CSFs improve the chances significantly"* is a probabilistic claim. **You cannot tick a CSF off; you either have it or you do not, throughout.**

**Grouped:**

| Cluster | CSFs |
|---|---|
| **Decisions before the project** | package and partner selection · clear goals · implementation strategy |
| **How the project is run** | project management · monitoring · team competence · software development |
| **The organisation around it** | **top management support · user involvement · interdepartmental communication · training and change management · organizational characteristics** |
| **What you work with** | ERP system · vendor support · environment |

> **The largest cluster is the organisation, not the project.**

---

**Reasons why ERP implementations succeed:** package selection well thought through against business requirements and long-term goals · **realistic and documented expectations** · **proper ROI justification** · caters to future needs, not just today's · **support of top management is of utmost importance** · **company's best brains work alongside the consultants** · **user acceptance is critical** · handling employee resistance · **training people at every level** · **communication is essential** · **an ERP project should not be viewed as an IT project but as a business project** · **minimize developments and customization; use the standard software** · adequate time for each activity · **the core team needs to be full time**

**Reasons why ERP implementations fail:** poor package selection · **inadequate requirement definition and unrealistic expectations, scope** · investment without ROI justification · not able to support changing business needs · **top management support lacking** · core team lacks the right resource · **user acceptance issues** · employees resist · training issues · **poor communication** · **project viewed as an IT project** · **customizing the software too much** · **too tight schedule, miscalculation of time and effort** · **high turnover rate of project team members**

**The two lists are the same list with the signs flipped** — fourteen one-to-one pairs. **That symmetry means there is no separate theory of failure: projects fail by the absence of the things that make them succeed.**

**The most quotable single line** is on user acceptance: ***"without that, even if the system goes LIVE, it will never be used by end users."*** **Go-live is not success.** A system that is technically live and practically bypassed has failed while appearing to have succeeded.

**Things to take care of:** **define measures of success** · managing project scope · requirements prioritization · **early success and pilots** · good relationship with vendor and partner · good project management · **clean data** · **quick decisions** · **test the solution thoroughly** · **sufficient budget till the end** · efficient risk management · **process owner's involvement** · **who owns business benefits**

⚠️ **Four of those deserve highlighting:**
- **"Define measures"** is first for a reason — Unit 2's Gartner finding was that **70% of failed ERP projects did not use performance metrics** and **27% did not measure at all**
- **"Early success and pilots"** buys credibility with sceptical users and with the steering committee — the same argument as the phased approach
- **"Quick decisions"** — ERP projects are **decision-dense**, and a decision that takes three weeks instead of three days idles a whole team
- **"Who owns business benefits"** — the project delivers a **system**; the **benefits** are realised afterwards, long after the team disbands. **If no named person owns them, nobody pursues them and the ROI justification quietly becomes fiction**

---

**The ranked failure percentages:**

| Reason | % |
|---|---|
| **Poor communication between relevant parties** | **57%** |
| **Lack of planning of scheduling, resources and activities** | **39%** |
| **No quality control** | **34%** |
| **Milestones not being set** | **29%** |
| **Inadequate co-ordination of resources** | **26%** |
| **Costs getting out of hand** *(**a symptom not a cause**)* | **20%** |
| **Mismanagement of progress** *(overlaps with poor communication)* | **17%** |
| Overall poor management | 13% |
| Suppliers skills overstretched | 12% |
| Supplier under-resourced | 11% |

**Three things about this table deserve comment:**

**① Communication leads at 57%** — nearly half again the second place, and *"mismanagement of progress" (17%)* **overlaps with it**, so the true figure is higher. **The number one cause of ERP failure is not technical.**

**② "Costs getting out of hand" is flagged as a symptom, not a cause.** Costs do not rise spontaneously — **they rise because scope changed, the schedule slipped, or rework was needed.** ⚠️ **Treating the cost overrun as the problem leads to the wrong remedy: cutting testing and training, which makes the actual causes worse.**

**③ The top five are all generic project-management failures** — precisely the *"risk associated with every project"* tier of the taxonomy.

$$\underbrace{57\% + 39\% + 34\% + 29\% + 26\%}_{\textbf{generic project management}} \gg \underbrace{12\% + 11\%}_{\textbf{supplier problems}}$$

---

**Real failed implementations:**

| Company | Package / Partner | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **W. L. Gore and Associates** | **PeopleSoft** / **Deloitte & Touche** | **October 1997: system went live; faulty. "Deloitte & Touche not experts"** |
| **FoxMeyer Drug Co.** | **SAP America** / **Anderson Consulting** | **Bankruptcy, 1998. "Could not handle the huge volume of transactions and had integration problems"** |
| **Cleveland State University** | **PeopleSoft** / **Kaludis Consulting Group** | **"Full of bugs; extra hardware"** |
| **Hershey** | **SAP AG R/3, 1999** / **IBM** | **"Bugs"** |

⚠️ **Every one of these names a Tier 1 package and a Tier 1 or 2 consulting firm. Choosing famous names is not a defence.**

**Map each to the framework:**

| Case | Failure mode | Framework item |
|---|---|---|
| **W. L. Gore** | *"not experts"* | **partner selection** — *industry experience, process consulting experience* |
| **FoxMeyer** | *"could not handle the huge volume"* | **package selection / functionality fit** — and **volume testing** |
| **Cleveland State** | *"bugs; extra hardware"* | **testing** and **technology scope** — hardware prerequisites are a contract clause |
| **Hershey** | *"bugs"*, 1999 | **testing** and **cutover** |

**FoxMeyer is the case worth knowing in detail** because the outcome was **bankruptcy** — the ERP project did not merely fail, it took the company with it. A drug distributor's entire business *is* high-volume transaction processing, so **a system that cannot process the volume is not a degraded system, it is no system.** In the risk vocabulary: **catastrophic — failure of primary mission.**

**Hershey's 1999 go-live is the standard cautionary tale about cutover timing** — it went live approaching its peak season, so the failure hit when the business could least absorb it. **Which is exactly why the cutover slide insists on understanding transaction criticality and making it a senior management decision.**

items.q: **Explain the change request management process, cutover, go-live and service level agreements.**
items.answer:
**Change Request Management Process — five steps:**
1. **User requests for a change**
2. **Impact of the same is analyzed and change is approved**
3. **Change is made in the development environment and transported to the quality environment**
4. **All documents (process and config docs) are updated with the change**
5. **Change is tested in the quality environment and transported to the production environment**

**The three-environment landscape:**

$$\textbf{Development} \xrightarrow{\textbf{Approval}} \textbf{Test / Quality} \xrightarrow{\textbf{Approval}} \textbf{Production}$$

| Environment | Purpose | Why it must be separate |
|---|---|---|
| **Development** | where the change is **made** | mistakes must be **free** — you break things while building |
| **Quality / Test** | where the change is **proved** | testing needs **stable, complete** data |
| **Production** | where the **business runs** | **nothing untested may ever touch it** |

**"Transported" is precise:** the change is not re-made in each environment — **the same object is moved forward, so what was tested is exactly what goes live.** **Two approval gates mean no change reaches production without passing test and being approved twice.**

⚠️ **Step 4 is deliberately placed *before* the final transport.** **Documentation is a precondition for going live, not a follow-up task** — a system whose documentation drifts from its configuration becomes unmaintainable.

**Three different needs for change requests:** **a vendor patch** (originates outside, you cannot refuse it indefinitely) · **a new business requirement** (originates inside — scope creep *during* the project, normal maintenance *after*) · **continuous improvement** (nobody asked; someone noticed a parameter could be better). **The same process handles all three, and that is intentional.**

---

**Cutover:**
- **The final stage of ERP Realization before the company moves to the new system**
- **Activities need to be planned in minute detail**
- **Transactions need to be stopped in the old application for a brief period and moved to the new ERP**
- **Cut over needs to be planned so there is minimum business disruption**
- **It is important to understand the criticality of the transaction before planning the cutover**

> *"There are some critical business transactions like **customer ordering, invoicing** which a business will never like to stop, as there may be chances of **revenue loss** — whereas something like **creating a maintenance order or creating new purchase contracts** can be deferred by a week."*

**The technical problem is small** — extract open items, load them into the new system. **But you can only extract them once the old system stops taking transactions**, and every hour it is stopped is an hour the business is not operating.

$$\textbf{cutover window} \propto \textbf{data volume} \qquad \textbf{business tolerance} \propto \frac{1}{\textbf{transaction criticality}}$$

⚠️ **The line that makes this a management problem:** *"typically **every department in the company believes their transactions are most critical**."* Ask each department and all will say they cannot stop. **Somebody with authority over all of them has to decide — which is why the deck says it must be a senior management decision.**

**This is also why cutover is scheduled over a weekend, a holiday or a period boundary** — you pick the moment when the fewest critical transactions are happening. **Hershey's 1999 peak-season go-live is the counter-example.**

---

**Go Live:**
- **The day a company moves from the old legacy system to the new ERP application**
- **Ideally all project activities complete before Go Live, though in most cases projects go live with a number of open issues**
- **It's OK to have such issues — till the company is not going live with some critical issues pending**
- **It's important to have a detailed list of these issues with an agreed-upon time frame within which they will be closed** by the consulting team and the core team
- **It is common to prepare a Go Live Checklist**

$$\textbf{go-live criterion} = \textbf{zero critical open items} + \textbf{a dated closure plan for the rest}$$

**"It's OK to have such issues" is a striking admission and the most useful sentence on the slide.** **Waiting for zero open issues means never going live** — new issues arrive faster than the tail closes. **But an undocumented open issue is not an open issue; it is a defect that has been forgotten.**

**The Go Live audit focuses on:** **completeness of integration testing · end user training · end user acceptance testing and signoff · data migration · support help desk · period end closing procedures · critical open items**

⚠️ **Five of its seven items are *readiness*, not *correctness*.** **At go-live, the risk is no longer that the system is wrong — it is that the organisation is not ready to use it.** *"Support help desk"* being an audit item is the sharpest instance: **go live without one and every user problem on day one has nowhere to go.**

---

**Service Contracts and SLAs:**
- **Service Contract:** **a long-term agreement with business partners specifying the services offered for that period**
- **SLA:** **contracts that assure the customer performance of certain services within a predefined period of time. SLAs list the level of service a customer is entitled to**

**An SLA can contain:**
- **Response time** — *call back within a specified time; technician on site within a specified time*
- **Service window / Availability time** — **working hours of the Support Center**
- **Downtime** — **maximum number of breakdowns per year**
- **Availability** — **percentage of assured system availability**
- **Solution time** — **maximum period allowed for the solution of a problem**

**The five parameters measure two different things:**

| Measures | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **How reliable is the system?** | **Downtime · Availability** |
| **How responsive is support?** | **Response time · Service window · Solution time** |

⚠️ **Response time and solution time are deliberately separate, and this is where SLAs are gamed.** *"We called you back within 15 minutes"* satisfies **response time** while the problem remains unsolved for a week. **Only solution time commits to actually fixing it** — so a support contract with a response-time SLA and no solution-time SLA is much weaker than it looks.

**Priority levels:** **SLAs are designed based on severity level. Issues of highest severity are Priority 1 (P1). For P1 and P2, support teams are available on call 24×7 on rotation. Priority 3 and 4 calls are generally attended the next business day.** **Service Level Reports (SLR) are prepared monthly to see SLA adherence.**

**The P1–P4 tiering is the same prioritisation principle as ABC, VED, risk impact levels and exception messages** — paying for round-the-clock cover on trivial issues is exactly the waste that severity tiers exist to avoid. **And the SLR closes the loop:** *"how you define success — define measures"* applied to the support phase, monthly and in writing. **Without it, an SLA is a promise nobody checks.**
